toc.title: Why a science theory got a bandwagon
How to scrutinize who you're listening to
Have I been part of the problem?

blocks.p: I love the Polyvagal Theory. I love it. It has answered so many questions for me, personally and professionally as a therapist and coach. Since learning about it in 2019, I've built this entire podcast on the foundation of my Polyvagal Theory knowledge. I've written three books, Stuck Not Broken books one through three. I created and run the [Unstucking Academy](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator). I've led workshops and keynotes. I've taught my fellow therapists. I'm also a member of the Polyvagal Institute's editorial board.

If you're also into the Polyvagal Theory, which I'm guessing you are, you've probably heard recently that it's dead. It's debunked. It's untenable. Its science is bad. It's not any of that, of course. But you've likely seen many self-proclaimed polyvagal-informed content creators turning their backs on the theory.

Between you and me, I'm okay with that. Very okay with that. No, the Polyvagal Theory is not dead or debunked or untenable. But I think, and I hope, the Polyvagal Theory bandwagon is. I'm going to look at whether the Polyvagal Theory has a bandwagon in the first place, why I think that bandwagon might be emptying, and why I think that's a very, very good thing that I am very excited about. Toward the end, I'll also take a look at myself, and how I've been a part of this whole bandwagon problem. Yes, I think I have been.

First, and importantly: what is a bandwagon? Very briefly, I define a bandwagon as a popular topic that people jump on just because it's popular. They get excited about it, and they ride the topic wherever it goes.

Bandwagon content creators learn about the topic superficially, enough to sound like they know what they're talking about, maybe using one of the ugly Polyvagal Theory resources out there. But their depth of knowledge isn't very deep, because they're only temporarily jumping on the bandwagon. They use the polyvagal buzzword and hashtag to create content for others interested in the topic, and they rake in the likes, the comments, the follows, and the ad revenue.

The important thing to note about Polyvagal Theory bandwagoners is that they not only jump on the bandwagon when it's popular, they also jump off when it's no longer popular, or seems to be declining in popularity. Or they go from polyvagal enthusiast bandwagoner to denier bandwagoner when it seems like the tide of popularity is shifting.

By the way, I'm not trying to be mean-spirited or start wellness influencer drama, so I'm not going to call anybody out by name. I'm not going to play clips of people saying one thing and now saying something else, like announcing that the Polyvagal Theory is dead, and I'm not going to show the blog articles where someone renounces the theory. I'm assuming you're already taking in polyvagal content from other people, and I'll leave it to you to scrutinize who you're listening to. I'll come back to that later.
Now that we agree on what a bandwagon is, the second question is: does the Polyvagal Theory have a bandwagon? I think it's pretty clear that it does. A bit of history to establish it.

The Polyvagal Theory first came to prominence in 1994, when Dr. Stephen Porges presented it in his presidential address to the Society for Psychophysiological Research. A few months later, I believe, the paper "Orienting in a Defensive World" came out in the journal Psychophysiology.

But before that, Porges had been working on pieces of what would become the Polyvagal Theory for decades. In 1969, he was working on heart rate variability to understand physiological states. In the seventies, he was studying newborns to evaluate heart rate as a measure of attention, orienting, and learning. In the eighties, his lab developed a means to accurately measure respiratory sinus arrhythmia, which becomes pretty important to the Polyvagal Theory as a measure of safety state activation.

None of this was the Polyvagal Theory as we know it now, but it was pieces of it, and it was getting closer, though at the time he didn't know that. Throughout these years, Porges was researching and writing numerous peer-reviewed papers. None of this late-sixties-to-1994 work was bandwagon, obviously. This was science stuff for science people, specifically about obstetrics and neonatology, focused on monitoring health risks in newborns. Very specific. Porges wasn't speaking or writing to therapists until after 1995, when he began researching individuals with autism and trauma.

In the late 1990s, he was frequently invited to present at mental health care provider meetings, giving keynotes that focused more on trauma. But even that isn't bandwagon. It was a relatively small group of clinicians who were early adopters of the theory and applied it to their clinical work. The early pioneers of applying the Polyvagal Theory to therapy were people like Peter Levine, the creator of Somatic Experiencing; Bessel van der Kolk, who invited Porges to give keynote addresses on trauma; and Pat Ogden, the creator of Sensorimotor Psychotherapy.

Again, none of this is bandwagon, but things obviously did change. The Polyvagal Theory's rather narrow focus was broadening at this time. And at some point, the Polyvagal Theory became a bandwagon, a popularity and content-creating explosion in the wellness realm of the internet.

The polyvagal bandwagon is obviously an internet phenomenon, so we can rule out anything before, say, 2001. And it's even more of a social media influencer and YouTube thing, so the bandwagon may have started as early as the mid-2010s. But I think it was a bit later.

As an aside, I spend pretty much zero time absorbing non-primary sources on the Polyvagal Theory. I don't listen to podcasts, watch YouTube content, or flick through short-form videos on the topic. So I'm kind of a terrible judge of when things get popular.

However, I started my podcast, which used to be named the Polyvagal Podcast, in 2019. At that time, there was already an audience hungry for information on the theory. I remember people messaging me to say how grateful they were to find so much accessible information on the topic in one place. They were kind of blown away. "There's a whole podcast just for the Polyvagal Theory?" They were stoked, to say the least. So the theory was at least growing in popularity in 2019. But I don't think the bandwagon had hit yet. If you look at Google searches from when I started in 2019, things were definitely on the uptick, but the spike hadn't happened yet.

I think the bandwagon began to hit in 2020, during the pandemic and the global societal turmoil. I think mental health problems were at an all-time high, whether it was reported or not, and people were online more often, searching for what the heck was happening within them. They had more time on their hands and more curiosity motivating them to try or learn novel things. We see a spike in Google searches during this time. There's a bigger spike in 2021, which I'm not quite sure about, but I think this is where the real bandwagon hit, and it has been more or less maintained since then.
We've seen a proliferation of content to meet this search demand across every medium: podcasts, YouTube, blogs, social media, and of course short-form videos.

Vagus nerve hacks, stimulation, resets, rewiring, or whatever the heck, came out of the internet woodwork from all angles and from everybody, it would seem. Rub your earlobe. Gargle. Put a frozen bag of peas on your chest, or cold raw meat in your bra. Jump in the cold pool. Extend your exhale. Hold your breath. Hold it for four seconds and release it for four. No, hold it for eight and release it for three. Some sort of box thing. Breathe faster. Breathe slower. Throw water in your face. Dance. Crane your neck at 45 degrees while stroking it. Hum with a voo. And on and on and on.

You've probably heard one or most of these. The people pushing this stuff will all tell you it somehow helps the vagus nerve. If you ask them how, they'll probably mutter something about the Polyvagal Theory. If you ask, "Yeah, but how?" they might say something about the safety system, or rest and digest, or parasympathetic something or other. But that's as far as they can take it, because they only have a very superficial understanding of the Polyvagal Theory, and they're riding the bandwagon of interest in it, or in the vagus nerve in general.

So these people run with their superficial understanding and write books, and create courses, and sell decks of cards and flip books and workbooks and board games, and on and on. Yes, I sell stuff too. You're right. We'll talk about that in a bit.
So can we agree that the Polyvagal Theory has a bandwagon? The timing doesn't matter so much, but it's there. I'd put it at 2020 to early 2026.

blocks.h: Why a science theory got a bandwagon

blocks.p: The next question is: why does the Polyvagal Theory have a bandwagon? The Polyvagal Theory is science. It's anatomy. It's neurological and bodily processes, brain stuff. It crosses over into evolution and embryology and measurements of things we won't understand or remember when asked, even if we do understand them. It's very difficult stuff.

So why would something like this have a bandwagon? If you only read Dr. Porges' primary writings, the theory would not have a bandwagon. It would have stayed in the realm of science, where it came from. It has a bandwagon because people realized they could apply it to their fields. People like Peter Levine, Bessel van der Kolk, and Pat Ogden made Porges' work accessible. They were the pioneers. They provided a platform for its integration into clinical practice.

And then Deb Dana made it really easy to understand. She translated it for us better than anybody had before her. She also gave us really easy-to-use, repeatable phrases: the polyvagal ladder, story follows state, home and away from home, glimmers and glows. So really, Deb Dana is to blame for the bandwagon. No, I'm kidding. Of course Deb's great. We love Deb. She's not to blame, but she definitely made it more accessible.

The heart of the Polyvagal Theory is not easy. Despite its many moving pieces, it fundamentally answers one question: the vagal paradox. In very simple language, the question is: how can the vagus nerve act as a friendly helper that keeps your body calm and healthy, but also be dangerous and slow your heart rate to an unhealthy, even potentially deadly, degree? How can one nerve do both of those things?

That's the heart of it, and it's kind of boring. Once it branches into the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems, which people have probably heard of, things become more interesting, especially the hypothesis that two parasympathetic systems use the vagus. But it's still kind of boring, in all honesty.

Once we start talking about safety and flight or fight and shutdown and freeze, well, now there's something we can latch onto. We've heard of those things before, and now we have a new way of understanding them, especially with cool phrases like story follows state and home and away from home.

So the rather boring, rather dry, rather difficult Polyvagal Theory became something rapidly accessible and repeatable. Combine that with internet and social media content-creation machines, and an unquenchable thirst for clicks, views, likes, shares, and ad revenue, and you've got the makings of a bandwagon.

You also have the audience for it. Not just clinicians like me, but anybody in the mind, body, or wellness space: yoga practitioners, doctors, psychiatrists, massage therapists, Reiki people, and on and on. Not just them, but also people who want to better understand those they serve, like teachers. And not only all of these people, but also people in need who are looking for answers. That's a lot of people, especially during a crisis like 2020.

Yes, the Polyvagal Theory is useful for all of these people. I think it has a place, at the very least in normalizing and giving words to their experiences: top-down understanding. That's what I keep hearing from my audience over and over again. And we can apply the knowledge to our work with our clients. It gives us a framework. I've built an entire self-regulation system around applying it.

But easily accessible knowledge, combined with easily repeatable and catchy phrases, combined with an audience desperate for understanding, creates the bandwagon garbage that people are spewing in one-minute clips.

So I think we've established the bandwagon, and we can see loosely how it developed. Now let's look at what might be happening, and what I personally hope, fingers crossed, is happening: bandwagon abandonment.

In early February 2026, a polyvagal critique paper was published. I use the word critique loosely here. It made waves in our little polyvagal world, to say the least. I was unaware of it, because I spend zero time consuming polyvagal content on social media and YouTube, but listeners of this podcast and Unstucking Academy students reached out to me for my thoughts. I gave them in episode 280, where I spell out what the critique still does not understand after 20 years.
It's at this point, February and March of 2026, that I think the Polyvagal Theory bandwagon has taken a major hit. I expect the bandwagon to have a mass exodus, at the very least. I hope it will.

We can already see content creators abandoning the bandwagon. They've announced the theory is dead and that they're moving on. In episode 280, I claimed that the critique paper is aimed at people like me, people in the clinical world, and I think I'm right. People who create content about the Polyvagal Theory are abandoning it because of this critique paper.

But I don't think they're abandoning the theory because they think the paper has validity. I think they're abandoning it because the paper appears to have validity, and these content creators don't understand the theory, or don't understand it well enough. They made content about the Polyvagal Theory when it was popular, with a superficial understanding. Now they're making content about the critique because it's popular, and because they never understood the Polyvagal Theory in enough depth in the first place to think critically about it.

These individuals, the ones who promoted it and are now abandoning it, are the bandwagon. And that bandwagon is exactly what made the theory's popularity vulnerable to a single critique paper. The version of the Polyvagal Theory most people encountered wasn't the real theory, or at least not in enough depth. The bandwagon influencer version of the theory is a watered-down game of telephone that cannot withstand scrutiny, because it was never built on a solid foundation to begin with.

So I think we have a perfect storm. Interest in the Polyvagal Theory is declining, according to Google search results and also YouTube searches. Google searches had their biggest plummet, it seems to me, in March: the biggest in forever. On top of the search drops, we have bandwagon influencers who never knew the topic well enough abandoning it. And we have relentless, misinformed criticism from one source undermining the theory's validity, getting those who don't understand it to hop off the bandwagon. Which is fine with me.

Now let's talk about Polyvagal Theory sources. Obviously it's important to get information from reliable sources. I'm sure you already know that. It's not that the Polyvagal Theory is flawed, although of course, in the science world, things are always up for discussion and always open to error. That's fine.

The issue is that most people have never actually encountered the real theory. They've encountered a copy of a copy of a copy, from content creators who need to pump out content and get their superficial understanding from other content being pumped out.
So let's think of sources as a hierarchy.

At the top is your firsthand source. That's Dr. Stephen Porges, who developed the theory: his published work, his lectures, his responses to criticism. I consider all of that the primary source material. And by the way, if you're wondering why Porges cites his own work so often, it's because he's the primary source. He's referring to his own peer-reviewed work. If you want to understand the theory deeply, Porges is where you eventually put your energy. But yes, it's very dense and very difficult to read by itself. So you may lean into interpretations of the primary work.

That brings us to secondhand sources. These are people who have studied the primary sources in depth, or trained directly with institutions affiliated with Porges' work, and who apply it rigorously in clinical or academic settings. I put myself here, in the second tier. I'm not trying to toot my own horn, but I'm very proud to have been asked to join the Polyvagal Institute's editorial board. I review other people's work specifically for accuracy with the theory. Toot toot. Deb Dana is in the second tier too, I'd say, although she might be more of a tier one-and-a-half source, given how closely she's worked with Porges over the years and continues to, with him and with the Polyvagal Institute.

Tier two is not just repeating what we read. We're translating it, but with a deeper working understanding of the original material, to what I think is a pretty healthy degree. And when a critique paper comes out, we don't run away. We read the paper. Not just read it: we understand it well enough. We compare it to what we know, and we respond with substance. We can show you, the audience, our thinking, and explain things in a way that makes sense, in our own words. Episode 280 is my attempt at this.

But in tier two, we do have limits to what we understand, of course. I'm a therapist. There's only so far I can take my understanding. I don't have Porges' phone number to double-check something, but I do have his primary documents, which I refer to all the time. So we in the second tier can get things wrong. I know I have.

Then you have thirdhand sources and beyond. Someone who read a blog post. Someone who attended a virtual seminar from someone else, who's maybe a second-tier source, but probably not. Someone who watched a few YouTube videos and is now "polyvagal informed." The further you get from the primary source, the more the signal degrades, even in the second tier I put myself in. Details get lost. Nuance disappears. Concepts get merged or oversimplified, and before you know it, you're learning something that barely resembles the actual theory, probably mixed with psychobabble and woo-woo on top. And you know how I feel about that stuff.

This is what happened. The polyvagal bandwagon was mostly built by thirdhand sources, and fourth, and fifth, and beyond. Now that there's been real critical pushback, even though it's very flimsy and a rehash of what has been said and rebutted for decades, a lot of those tier-three-and-beyond people don't have the foundational knowledge and understanding to respond. They can't defend what they were teaching, because they never fully understood it in the first place. So they leave. They move on to the next framework, perhaps searching for the next bandwagon. And sadly, the Polyvagal Theory takes the reputational hit for their shallow understanding.
But this is all good. I find this all very good, and I sincerely hope there is a major bandwagon abandonment happening. Now the serious work can continue.

If we see more influencers leaving, more polyvagal-informed accounts going quiet, more psychologists proclaiming that the theory is dead or wrong or debunked or untenable, more drops in search traffic and curiosity, that's not evidence that the theory is failing. That's evidence that the market is correcting itself. The bandwagon is emptying. The hype cycle may be ending after five years, and what's left after the hype is what actually matters.

What's left are the people who did, and are doing, the real work, not the superficial content-creation work. The people who read the primary documents deeply enough to understand them, not just so they can say they read them when they make their content with clever thumbnails and titles. The people who stuck around because the theory holds up under scrutiny, not because it was getting likes.

This bandwagon abandonment would be a good thing. It would mean the conversations around the Polyvagal Theory can finally get even more honest, more accurate, and more useful. The noise, the content clutter, may be fading, and less content will come out as a result. At least, I really hope so. I hope to see the Google search results continue to plummet. That would signal less superficial interest in the theory, and less superficial content about it as a result. Bandwagoners follow trends, so content should drop as demand drops, and demand should drop as content creators abandon the theory.
You're here, and you've gotten this far, because you take this stuff seriously. We need more of you, and I hope to keep earning your trust in what I create.

My hope is that the Polyvagal Theory enters another period in which only people who take it seriously and build on deep knowledge are involved. I missed out on the late nineties, when the Polyvagal Theory was just starting to integrate into the therapy world. I was too busy catching Pokémon, watching Seinfeld, hypnotizing my friends, and stealing Star Wars prequel merchandise. I was in high school, by the way. My hope is that we might enter another period like that, where it's more niche and less watered down.

I don't want to serve people, as a therapist or as a coach, who are looking for vagus nerve hacks. That's silly. I want people like you, I'm assuming, who are serious about learning and serious about applying.

So yes, I'm glad the polyvagal bandwagon may be dying. I sincerely want more tier-three-and-beyond creators to announce that the theory is dead, or has bad science, or is debunked, or whatever. And I really hope they keep up their old videos, posts, and blogs where they raved about the Polyvagal Theory. Let's keep those receipts there for everyone to see. Not as a way to shame, but as a way to check someone's credibility, as a way to screen them. I imagine they'll keep it all up anyway, so they can keep getting ad revenue from both their praise of the Polyvagal Theory and their abandonment of it. They can capture both click sources.

blocks.h: How to scrutinize who you're listening to

blocks.p: I think this potential bandwagon abandonment is great for you, the listener. I hope there's less for you to sift through and try to make sense of.

I invite you to scrutinize those who are jumping off the bandwagon, and check their past content. Look at the dates. Notice whether they actually explain the rationale for their choice to abandon the theory, or whether they may be intimidated by polyvagal misunderstandings and a fake scientific consensus. That's not how consensus works, by the way. And it's okay if they are intimidated, but they should probably be honest and transparent about it.

Notice whether those content creators are able to share their decisions, and why they made them, in their own language. Notice whether they're just trying to soothe you about the criticisms, or inviting you to understand along with them, again in their own language. Notice whether they hang on to whatever they like about the Polyvagal Theory but stop talking about it.

blocks.h: Have I been part of the problem?

blocks.p: So have I been a part of the Polyvagal Theory bandwagon problem? Kind of, yes. I've been creating free polyvagal-informed content for over seven years now. I use easy-to-understand, repeatable phrases. I've created coursework. I've written three books. I have a blog. You get the idea.

Like I said at the beginning, I love the Polyvagal Theory. I started the podcast seven years ago after I heard a very dry and boring lecture from Dr. Porges on YouTube. Then Deb Dana made it make sense. Then Peter Levine helped me understand how it applies to the somatic components of clinical practice, which I had not even been exposed to before. I consider these three my polyvagal trinity, and I did the majority of my early learning from them. I've read a lot of Porges' primary work. I don't listen to any third-tier sources, and honestly, it gives me a significant ick factor when I try. It's a very visceral, body-contorting "ugh" for me.
Over the years, I've been on numerous podcasts, big and small, all third-tier sources and beyond, to talk about the Polyvagal Theory in simple terms with repeatable language.

I didn't start this podcast because the theory was getting popular. I didn't even know it was popular. I found the theory because I was struggling with traumatized clients, and I was researching trauma on YouTube, starting from scratch, to see what I was missing. There was something I just didn't understand, and I was trying to figure it out. That's how I found the Polyvagal Theory: not through a hashtag or an algorithm.

I got so immersed in the theory, in its primary sources, and in Deb Dana and Peter Levine, that I started teaching my fellow therapists at work about it, and then giving presentations on it when I was working in the public school system. No likes, no clicks, no ad revenue. Just sharing what I was passionate about.

Then I started the podcast. The Polyvagal Institute reached out to me and a few others, I think a couple of years ago, to join their editorial board, where we review submissions for polyvagal accuracy. I happily accepted, not because of the pay, because there is none. We're volunteers. I accepted because I want to scrutinize the heck out of people's work on the Polyvagal Theory and make sure it's accurate. I really enjoy doing that. It's important to me that the information is accurate, especially if it's going out to you.

By the way, do you want to know how many polyvagal-informed influencers reached out to the Polyvagal Institute for clarity on the recent criticisms? If you guessed zero, you're correct. Sadly, zero of them reached out to us for comment.

Anyhow, I have gotten things wrong. I'm sure of it. Early on, I referred to shutdown and freeze as if they were the same thing, until I spoke directly with Dr. Porges in episode 15. I've probably said that only mammals are social, or something along those lines. So yes, I've contributed to the bandwagon. But I think I've done so as a responsible and reputable source, and I plan to keep doing so. I've corrected what I got wrong.

Nothing has changed in what I'm doing here or how I want to show up for you. This started as a polyvagal podcast, and at its heart it still is, even when I'm discussing the research on EMDR, or sharing my thoughts on how shutdown affects the partner in a relationship. Stuck Not Broken was not, and is not, a generic psychology podcast, or even a generic nervous system podcast that integrated the Polyvagal Theory while it was popular.
Ultimately, it's up to you to scrutinize me and others and decide whether we're a solid source of information. I know what I think about me, and I hope I've earned your trust.

My commitment to you has always been the same. I'm going to give you information that is as polyvagal informed, as accurate, and as nuanced as I possibly can, along with how it applies to your life, your unstucking process, your self-development, and your understanding of yourself. Just like I would for my own life.

The Polyvagal Theory definitely has a place in discussion. We should discuss it and we should scrutinize it, but not all content creators are doing that in the same way. Some are simply more responsible than others. Some are simply more trustworthy than others.

You're not going to hear me tout the benefits of earlobe stroking, or neck craning, or gargling, or putting raw meat in your bra. You won't hear me hype vagus nerve stimulators, vagus hacking, or resetting your nervous system in four easy steps. In my opinion, these are all red flags. You and I take this seriously. We know there are no hacks and no shortcuts, so we should treat things that way. Let's be serious about what we know and what questions we have, and move forward together.

The Polyvagal Theory is not dead, but its bandwagon might be. The Polyvagal Theory is not untenable; its criticisms, and again I use that word loosely, are. The Polyvagal Theory's science doesn't have a problem that I know of. The superficial content-creator understanding of it does.

The bandwagon is hopefully dying. Good. Now we can do the real work. Now we can focus on applying this in a way that's actually meaningful. Or rather, continue to. We've been doing that for the past seven years, and we'll keep doing it.
